name: Kingdom of Aksum
summary: A trading kingdom of the Horn of Africa that minted its own coins, built giant stelae and adopted Christianity in the 4th century.

knownFor.label: Giant stelae
knownFor.note: Carved granite obelisks up to about 33 m tall.

knownFor.label: Aksumite coins
knownFor.note: One of the first African states to mint its own coins.

knownFor.label: Ge‘ez script
knownFor.note: A script still used in the Ethiopian church.

location.value: The Horn of Africa (today’s Eritrea and northern Ethiopia), and at times South Arabia (Yemen). The capital was Axum.

terrain.value: Highlands with fertile soils, linked to the Red Sea port of Adulis.
terrain.source: Munro-Hay, Aksum: An African Civilisation of Late Antiquity (1991)

climate.value: Highland climate with summer rains, cooler than the lowlands.

resources.value: Ivory, gold, incense, teff, barley and wheat, salt and cattle.

disasters.value: Soil erosion and environmental decline (around 650–700) are suggested factors in its decline.

population.value: Not known; the city of Aksum may have had about 20,000 people.
population.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Aksum (checked 6 Nov 2026) (not stated)

urbanisation.value: Axum was a major city with palaces and stelae. Later the capital moved to Kubar (after about 800).

disease.value: Not documented in the sources checked.

migration.value: Beja peoples moved into the Eritrean plateau in the late 7th century.

economicBase.value: Agriculture and long-distance trade, which made Aksum a major commercial power.

tradeRoutes.value: Controlled Red Sea and Indian Ocean trade between Rome and India: ivory, gold and tortoiseshell were exported, and silk and spices imported.

wealth.value: No estimate exists. The prophet Mani ranked Aksum among the four great powers of the 3rd century, with Persia, Rome and China.

moneyAndTax.value: One of the first African states to mint its own coins (gold, silver, bronze), from King Endybis (late 3rd century).

inequality.value: Kings and nobles (buried in stone tombs) above commoners. Slaves were traded.

governmentType.value: A monarchy under the negusa nagast (“king of kings”), possibly ruling a confederation of local rulers.

keyRulers.value: Gedara (c. 200–230). Endybis (first coins). Ezana (4th century, converted to Christianity). Kaleb (c. 514–542, peak). Dil Na’od (last, 10th century).

succession.value: Hereditary monarchy. The details are uncertain.

institutions.value: Geʿez was made the official language under Ezana. Greek was used in diplomacy.

stability.value: Long-lived, but it lost Yemen to Persia (570s) and faced revolts in South Arabia.

eliteConflict.value: Abraha, an Aksumite general in Yemen, broke away (c. 525) and ruled independently.

armyAndTech.value: Armies that crossed the Red Sea to Arabia, and campaigned in Nubia.
armyAndTech.source: Munro-Hay, Aksum: An African Civilisation of Late Antiquity (1991)

majorWars.value: Ezana’s conquest of Kush (Meroë, c. 330). Kaleb’s invasion of Himyar (Yemen, 518–525). The Aksumite–Persian wars (570–578).

territoryChange.value: About 1.25 million km² (350), rising to about 2.5 million km² (525) at its height (Wikipedia infobox).

alliancesRivals.value: An ally of the Byzantine Empire (fellow Christians). Rivals: Himyar, Kush and Persia.

inventions.value: Giant carved granite stelae (the largest about 33 m tall), terraced farming and coinage.

scienceEducation.value: The Geʿez script developed into an abugida (with vowels). Early Christian manuscripts include the Garima Gospels.

openness.value: Open to Roman, Indian and Arabian trade and ideas. It received Christianity from Syrian missionaries (Frumentius).

religion.value: Traditional Aksumite religion, then Christianity, adopted under King Ezana in the 4th century (c. 325–340), one of the earliest Christian states.

languageWriting.value: Geʿez, Sabaic and Greek. The Geʿez script is still used today in Ethiopia and Eritrea.

artsArchitecture.value: Monumental stelae, palaces (e.g. Dungur), coins, and early churches.

socialStructure.value: King, nobles, farmers and traders, and slaves.

sharedIdentity.value: Christianity and Geʿez culture, later claimed by Ethiopia’s Solomonic dynasty.
sharedIdentity.source: Munro-Hay, Aksum: An African Civilisation of Late Antiquity (1991)

neighbours.value: Kush/Nubia, Himyar (Yemen), the Roman and Byzantine Empires, Persia, and Arabia.

ideasReligions.value: Gave refuge to early Muslims in the First Hijra (613–615), and spread Christianity in the Horn of Africa.

colonisation.value: Ruled parts of South Arabia (Yemen) in the 3rd and 6th centuries.

riseSignals.value: Emerging from the earlier Dʿmt culture, control of Red Sea trade, coinage, and conquest.

peakPeriod.value: The 4th–6th centuries, under Ezana and Kaleb.

declineSignals.value: The loss of Yemen (570s), Islamic expansion cutting trade routes (7th century), Beja migration and soil erosion.

outcome.value: Decline and collapse around 960, in uncertain circumstances (traditionally linked to the disputed Queen Gudit). Succeeded by the Zagwe dynasty, and later the Solomonic Ethiopian Empire.

sources.value: Inscriptions, coins, stelae, Greek and Roman accounts (the Periplus), and later Ethiopian tradition. Checked against Wikipedia on 6 Nov 2026. See also Munro-Hay (1991).

overallCertainty.value: Low to moderate. Dates of conversion (c. 324–340), coinage and the end are debated. Second source: Wikidata starts it c. 400 BCE (including the earlier Dʿmt period); Wikipedia says founded in the 1st century CE.
